teaser: A snake's jaws, a hand's width from an old man's head: El Greco's only painting of a myth.
review_notes:
Usually dated about 1610-1614; El Greco's only surviving mythological subject.
The 1614 inventory of his studio lists three Laocoon pictures; this is the only one known today.
The third head (and an extra leg) at the right were uncovered when later overpaint was removed in a 1950s cleaning: per National Gallery of Art accounts; exact date of treatment to confirm.
The city gate the horse trots toward is usually identified as Toledo's Bisagra Gate.
The local legend that Toledo was founded by descendants of Trojans is often cited as a reason for the setting; it is an interpretation.
Identities proposed for the right-hand figures include Apollo and Artemis, Poseidon and Cassandra, Adam and Eve.
Quote 'I fear the Greeks, even when they bring gifts' is the usual English rendering of Virgil, Aeneid, Book 2.
Size about 137.5 x 172.5 cm. Samuel H. Kress Collection, at the National Gallery of Art since 1946.

lesson.text: The bite has not landed yet. In the middle of this canvas an old man lies on his back and grips a snake just below its head. He holds it at arm's length, and the open jaws hang a hand's width from his skull. His eyes are locked on them. Everything in the painting waits on that small gap.

The man is Laocoön, a priest of the ancient city of Troy. In the old story, Greek soldiers have besieged Troy for ten years. One morning they are gone, and a giant wooden horse stands outside the walls. Laocoön begs his people not to bring it in. “I fear the Greeks, even when they bring gifts,” he says in the Roman poet Virgil's telling.

He is right: the horse is hollow and full of soldiers. But the gods have already chosen the Greek side. They send two sea serpents to silence the priest, and his two sons with him. The Trojans take it as a sign that he was lying, and drag the horse inside. El Greco stops the story a breath before the end.

lesson.title: Three stages of one death
lesson.text: Father and sons are each at a different point of the same fight. Read them from left to right.

spots.title: Still fighting
spots.text: One son stands and wrestles a serpent that loops around him in a great dark ring. Both hands grip its body. His head is thrown back, and he has not lost yet.

spots.title: The gap
spots.text: The snake's head, mouth open, is held just short of Laocoön's gray hair. His wide eyes stare straight at it. This is the frozen instant.

spots.title: Already over
spots.text: The second son lies upside down toward us, legs in the air, head and limp arm at the bottom. For him the fight has ended.

lesson.text: A painting can show only one moment, so El Greco packs three into it: the struggle, the last second, and the aftermath, laid side by side like frames of a film.

The most famous Laocoön is a marble sculpture carved in ancient times and dug out of a vineyard in Rome in 1506. It caused a sensation, and artists flocked to draw it. El Greco lived in Rome in the 1570s and surely knew it.

In the marble, father and sons are locked together in one knot of muscle. El Greco, some forty years after leaving Rome, pulls the knot apart. He scatters the bodies across a dark rock and gives each one room. And he paints flesh no sculptor would recognize: gray-white, lit as if by a storm, with shadows of blue and green.

The bodies are also too long. Legs and torsos are stretched well past natural proportions, which makes the figures look weightless, almost like smoke. This taste for elegant distortion over accuracy has a name: Mannerism, a style that spread across Europe in the 1500s. El Greco pushed it further than almost anyone.
Now look past the bodies to the sunlit town in the distance. Troy stood on the coast of what is now Turkey. This town has a different skyline, and one very small visitor is on its way in.
The wooden horse of the story is in the picture, though it looks very much alive. Can you find it?

spots.title: The horse
spots.text: A small golden-brown horse trots along the road toward a city gate. Nobody stops it. While the priest dies in the foreground, his warning is already being ignored.

lesson.text: And the city it trots toward is not Troy at all. It is Toledo, the Spanish town where El Greco lived for almost forty years, complete with one of its real gates. An old local legend claimed that Toledo had been founded by descendants of Trojans. Perhaps that is the link. Or perhaps he was warning his own neighbors about something.

As far as we know, this is the only subject from ancient myth El Greco ever painted. Nearly everything else he made was religious pictures and portraits, which is what Spanish buyers of his day wanted.

He seems to have painted it for himself. No client is recorded, and the canvas was still in his studio when he died in 1614. A list of his belongings mentions three pictures of Laocoön. This is the only one anyone has seen since, and parts of it look unfinished, above all the right-hand edge.

Two pale figures stand there, calmly watching. They are not in Virgil's story. Are they gods who came to see their sentence carried out? Nobody knows. And when restorers cleaned the canvas in the 20th century, they found that these two had company.

lesson.title: The watchers
lesson.text: The group at the right edge holds the painting's biggest puzzle.

spots.title: The onlookers
spots.text: One figure shows us its back and turns its head toward the scene. The other faces us and looks away. Neither moves to help.

spots.title: One head too many
spots.text: Between the two heads is a third face in profile, with no body of its own. A later hand had painted over it. Cleaning brought it back.

lesson.text: The extra head is probably a change of mind. El Greco may have tried the figure one way, then another, and died before choosing. Later owners tidied the area by covering the leftover parts. Today the museum leaves both versions visible, so you see the painter mid-decision.
Scholars have proposed many names for the watchers, among them the gods Apollo and Artemis, and even Adam and Eve. None of the guesses has won.
The picture is doubly suspended. The story stops one second before the bite, and the painting itself stops before its maker was done. Neither one ever gets its ending.

quiz.question: What exact instant does the painting freeze?
options: The moment just before the snake bites Laocoön
quiz.explanation: Laocoön holds the snake's open jaws a hand's width from his head.

quiz.question: Why was Laocoön punished?
options: He warned the Trojans against the wooden horse
quiz.explanation: The gods, siding with the Greeks, sent serpents to silence his warning.

quiz.question: Which city appears in the background?
quiz.explanation: Instead of Troy he painted the Spanish city he had lived in for almost forty years.

quiz.question: What did the cleaning of the canvas reveal on the right?
options: A third head between the two onlookers
quiz.explanation: A face that had been painted over reappeared between the two standing figures.

quiz.question: What is Mannerism, as seen in these bodies?
options: A style that prefers elegant distortion, such as stretched limbs, to accuracy
A way of painting only in black and white
The exact copying of ancient statues
quiz.explanation: The elongated, weightless figures are typical of this 1500s style.

facts.text: El Greco painted dozens of scenes from ancient myth.
facts.explanation: This is the only mythological subject he is known to have painted.

facts.text: The painting was still in El Greco's studio when he died.
facts.explanation: No client is recorded, and it stayed with him until his death in 1614.

facts.text: The Trojan horse appears as a huge wooden machine filling the background.
facts.explanation: It is a tiny, living-looking horse trotting toward the city gate.
